quickAnswer: Beylerbeyi Palace offers an intimate 19th-century Ottoman summer residence on Istanbul's Asian shore—open Tuesday through Sunday from 09:00 to 17:30 and closed Mondays—with far shorter queues than Dolmabahçe. body.text: How does Beylerbeyi Palace compare to Dolmabahçe?

Commissioned by Sultan Abdülaziz between 1863 and 1865 as a summer retreat and state guesthouse, Beylerbeyi Palace is smaller, calmer, and easier to absorb in 60 to 90 minutes than sprawling Dolmabahçe across the water. Its 24 rooms and six halls blend Neo-Baroque stonework with traditional Ottoman house layouts, Egyptian reed matting, Hereke carpets, and Baccarat crystal chandeliers ([Milli Saraylar Official Page](https://www.millisaraylar.gov.tr/Lokasyon/4/Beylerbeyi-Sarayi)).

Where Dolmabahçe overwhelms with sheer administrative scale, Beylerbeyi feels personal. Its central ground-floor hall cools the interior with an indoor marble fountain pool, while ceilings carry nautical motifs reflecting Sultan Abdülaziz's passion for the Ottoman navy. Visiting monarchs—including Empress Eugénie of France and Emperor Franz Joseph of Austria-Hungary—stayed here, and deposed Sultan Abdülhamid II spent his final six years inside before his death in 1918. Foreign visitor tickets are listed at 800 TL (200 TL domestic; 100 TL garden-only), though always check [Milli Saraylar](https://www.millisaraylar.gov.tr/Lokasyon/4/Beylerbeyi-Sarayi) before traveling as Turkish lira tariffs adjust periodically.

body.text: Beylerbeyi Palace is closed every Monday, as well as on New Year's Day (January 1) and the first day of both Ramadan Bayram and Kurban Bayram ([Milli Saraylar Visiting Hours](https://www.millisaraylar.gov.tr/Lokasyon/4/Beylerbeyi-Sarayi)). On open days (Tuesday through Sunday), the palace operates from 09:00 to 17:30, with the ticket office closing at 17:00.

Note that if a national or religious holiday falls on a Monday, the palace remains closed. Also keep in mind that while the main palace building (Mâbeyn and Harem) and waterfront gardens are open to visitors, the upper-terrace Marble, Yellow, and Stable Pavilions remain closed to general admission. Interior photography is prohibited, and shoe covers are provided at the door.
Why is Kuzguncuk famous for its wooden houses, church, mosque and synagogue?

Just 1.5 kilometers south of Beylerbeyi, [Kuzguncuk](https://visit.istanbul/kuzguncuk) preserves one of Istanbul's clearest architectural records of Ottoman-era multi-faith neighborhood life. Pastel-painted timber row houses line leafy İcadiye Caddesi, while the Armenian Surp Krikor Lusavoriç Church stands wall-to-wall beside Kuzguncuk Mosque on the coastal road, steps from the Beth Yaakov Synagogue and historic Greek Orthodox churches ([Üsküdar Municipality Kuzguncuk Guide](https://www.uskudar.bel.tr/userfiles/files/2019/Kuzguncuk%20.pdf)).

Sephardic Jewish, Armenian, Greek, and Turkish families lived here side by side for centuries; local accounts note that the Armenian community even donated part of its land so the neighboring mosque could be built beside their church. Today, İcadiye Caddesi feels like a quiet village high street filled with bakeries, small bookshops, ceramic studios, and the historic community vegetable garden (Kuzguncuk Bostanı). Strolling from the waterfront up İcadiye and back down Perihan Abla Sokağı takes about an hour at an easy pace.
How do you combine both with Çengelköy tea gardens?

Link all three Asian-shore neighborhoods in a single northbound loop from Üsküdar—starting with morning coffee in Kuzguncuk, touring Beylerbeyi Palace before midday, and finishing with tea and simit under the centuries-old plane tree at Çengelköy's Tarihi Çınaraltı ([Çengelköy Neighborhood Guide](https://wowcappadocia.com/cengelkoy-istanbul.html)).

items: 09:00 Kuzguncuk arrival: Take the ferry to Üsküdar (or the direct [Şehir Hatları Bosphorus commuter ferry](https://sehirhatlari.istanbul/en/timetables/domestic-trips/lines/to-bosphorus-from-bosphorus-167) to Kuzguncuk Pier) and walk İcadiye Caddesi before brunch tables fill up.
10:30 Beylerbeyi Palace: Walk 20 minutes north along the coastal road—or ride any Üsküdar–Beykoz bus two stops—to tour the palace and its shaded magnolia gardens.

12:30 Çengelköy tea garden: Continue 25 minutes north on foot (or five minutes by bus 15) to Çengelköy's waterfront; pick up hot börek from a neighborhood bakery and bring it into Tarihi Çınaraltı, where guests are welcome to eat outside pastries alongside freshly brewed tea.
14:30 Ferry return: Check the afternoon Şehir Hatları sailing directly from Çengelköy Pier back to Eminönü or Beşiktaş, or take a short bus south to Üsküdar Marmaray station.

faq.q: Is Beylerbeyi Palace covered by Museum Pass Istanbul or Türkiye?
faq.a: National Palaces (Milli Saraylar) sites follow separate ticketing rules from Ministry of Culture museums; confirm current pass validity at the Beylerbeyi box office or on [millisaraylar.gov.tr](https://www.millisaraylar.gov.tr/Lokasyon/4/Beylerbeyi-Sarayi) before your visit.

faq.q: Can you take photos inside Beylerbeyi Palace?
faq.a: No. Photography and video are prohibited inside the palace rooms, though you may photograph the exterior marble facade and waterfront gardens.

faq.q: Can visitors enter the synagogue and churches in Kuzguncuk?
faq.a: Kuzguncuk Mosque is open outside prayer times; the Armenian and Greek churches open mainly for services or limited morning hours, while Beth Yaakov Synagogue requires advance security permission from the Chief Rabbinate foundation.

faq.q: How do I get from Eminönü or Beşiktaş to Kuzguncuk?
faq.a: Take a frequent ferry to Üsküdar (10–20 minutes) and walk 20 minutes north along the Bosphorus road or ride a 5-minute bus, or catch a direct Şehir Hatları Bosphorus commuter sailing to Kuzguncuk Pier.

faq.q: Is Tarihi Çınaraltı in Çengelköy open all year?
faq.a: Yes. The waterfront tea garden operates daily year-round, with sheltered seating in cooler months and open Bosphorus tables from spring through autumn.

faq.q: What is the best day of the week to visit Beylerbeyi and Kuzguncuk?
faq.a: Tuesday through Friday mornings offer the quietest streets in Kuzguncuk and short entry lines at Beylerbeyi Palace; avoid Mondays because the palace is closed.
